title: Lindsay Clancy’s retrial scheduled for March 2027 | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother who argues she should not be held criminally responsible for killing her three children, is slated to face a second trial beginning on March 29, 2027, less than a year after her first trial ended with a hung jury.

Prosecutors said in court Monday the charges require a jury trial. That appeared to indicate they intend to retry Clancy on the same charges of first-degree murder, which requires a jury trial.

“The die has been cast,” defense attorney Kevin Reddington said. “I think you can read between the lines that when they say the case is going to require a jury, that it’s an indirect comment from the (District Attorney) that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments.”

In herfirst trial, Clancy faced three counts of first-degree murder, though the jury was able to consider lesser charges in their deliberations. The judge declared a mistrial after the jury deadlocked, with one holdout juror preventing the panel from finding Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility.

Deciding on a trial date Monday led to some frustration among the prosecution, defense and judge, with the defense pushing for an earlier date and the prosecution concerned about the scheduling of other murder trials. The court also set pre-trial hearings for December 30 and February 18.

The prosecution’s decision to retry Clancy is the latest development in the triple-murder case that became one of the most debated criminal trials in recent memory this summer before it ended in a mistrial.

Prosecutors have argued Clancy, 36, “acted intentionally, rationally and swiftly” when she fatally strangled her three children in their Duxbury home and attempted suicide in January 2023. Her defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.

Legal experts cautioned the retrial is not set in stone and could be altered by prosecutorial decisions orplea negotiationsbefore the start of the trial.

“Monday will be significant in that it would be a signal about the prosecution’s big picture decision about whether it wants to pursue criminal charges as opposed to dismissing them,” Daniel Medwed, a professor of law and criminal justice at Northeastern University School of Law, told CNN prior to Monday’s hearing.

“But what happens on Monday is the beginning, not the end, because a lot of different things could happen in the run-up to trial.”

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz, who could initiate plea negotiations, did not appear in court Monday. CNN has reached out to his office for further information.

Outside court, Reddington said he did not believe a plea deal was possible. “I don’t think they’d give me the right time of day at this point,” he said.

Separately, Clancy’s defense filed an appeal Monday before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, asking it to overturn Judge William Sullivan’s ruling rejecting her motion to dismiss the charges – a decision that paved the way for the retrial.

Clancy’s attorneys have argued, in part, that a retrial would violate her constitutional protections against double jeopardy.

Clancy’s trial this summer featured emotional testimony from her ex-husband,Patrick, family members and friends,Clancy’s doctorsand psychiatric experts.

The prosecution argued that Clancy’s actions before the killings, including sending her husband out of the house on errands, show she knew what she was doing when she killed her children.

In contrast, Clancy has said in court filings and interviews with psychiatric experts that she heard amale voice directing herto kill her children and then herself and lost control of her actions.

The case put a spotlight onmaternal mental health, postpartum psychosis, theinternet’s tendency toward conspiracyand the ongoing skepticism of the so-called “insanity defense.”

After more than a month of testimony, the 12-person jury was unable to come to a unanimous decision due to alone holdout juror. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial due to the deadlock, setting up the possibility of a retrial with a new jury.

Still, the jury’s 11-1 split in favor of not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility indicated that prosecutors could face an uphill battle in a retrial.

Clancy did not testify in the trial. She has been held in Tewksbury Hospital since shortly after the killings and remains partially paralyzed due to her suicide attempt.

She could face life in prison if convicted of murder. If jurors find she cannot be held criminally responsible, the court will likely begin the process of committing her to a psychiatric hospital.

Since the mistrial, Reddington filed a series of motions seeking to prevent a retrial, but Sullivan rejected each of them in turn.

In a retrial, the case starts over with a new jury, prosecutors and the defense make their arguments and witnesses take the stand and testify. In general, a retrial can be quite similar to the original trial, although the parties may drop weaker arguments and focus more on their stronger evidence.

Reddington said Monday he believed the defense might have an advantage in this retrial.

“We’ve already had a dry run. We know what their case is. We know (who) their witnesses are,” he said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Nicki Brown reported from Plymouth, Massachusetts, while Eric Levenson reported from New York. CNN’s Lauren del Valle contributed to this report.
